reference.source: Braddom's Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation / pain medicine references
clinicalPearls: Myofascial pain syndrome is a regional pain disorder characterised by myofascial trigger points, which are hyperirritable spots within a palpable taut band of skeletal muscle
Pressing a trigger point reproduces the patient's familiar pain and refers it in a characteristic, reproducible pattern that does not follow dermatomal boundaries
A local twitch response, elicited by snapping palpation or needling of the taut band, supports the diagnosis, which is fundamentally clinical
It is distinguished from fibromyalgia, which is a widespread pain disorder with diffuse tender points rather than regional referring trigger points
Perpetuating factors such as poor posture, ergonomic strain, muscle overload, and underlying structural or psychological stressors should be identified and corrected
Core treatment is manual and physical therapy including trigger-point release, stretching, spray-and-stretch techniques, and posture and activity correction
Trigger-point injection or dry needling can deactivate stubborn points, and botulinum toxin injection is used for selected refractory cases
Addressing sleep, mood, and contributing chronic conditions improves durability of the response, and long-term management emphasises self-directed exercise
reference.pathophysiology: Myofascial trigger points are thought to develop where sustained or repetitive muscle overload leads to localised areas of contracted sarcomeres and a taut band. A widely cited model proposes excessive acetylcholine release at dysfunctional motor endplates, producing sustained contraction, local ischaemia and energy crisis, and accumulation of sensitising biochemical mediators. This lowers the local pain threshold, sensitises peripheral nociceptors, and, through convergence in the dorsal horn, generates referred pain and contributes to central sensitisation when the process becomes chronic.
additionalDifferentials: Cervical or lumbar facet joint pain
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination to locate taut bands, trigger points, and reproducible referred pain
Assessment of posture, ergonomics, and mechanical perpetuating factors
Investigations to exclude mimics, such as imaging or nerve conduction studies when a structural or neurological cause is suspected
Screening for contributing conditions including thyroid dysfunction, vitamin deficiency, and sleep disturbance
Blood tests such as inflammatory markers where inflammatory or systemic disease is considered
redFlags: Constitutional features such as fever, weight loss, or night sweats suggesting infection or malignancy
Progressive neurological deficit indicating a radicular or cord lesion rather than muscular pain
Sudden severe pain or a mass suggesting an alternative acute pathology
Pain unresponsive to appropriate myofascial treatment prompting review of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Acute myofascial pain from an identifiable overload often resolves well when the trigger points are treated and perpetuating factors corrected. Chronic cases with central sensitisation and unaddressed contributing factors can be persistent, but most patients improve with an active, multimodal rehabilitation approach.
pitfalls: Mislabelling widespread fibromyalgia as regional myofascial pain, or vice versa
Treating trigger points while ignoring the posture, ergonomic, or structural factors that perpetuate them
Relying on passive treatments and medication without an active exercise programme
Overlooking sleep disturbance, mood, and stress that maintain chronic muscle pain
Repeated needling of trigger points without addressing the underlying cause
management: Base treatment on manual and physical therapy including trigger-point release, stretching and spray-and-stretch techniques
Perform trigger-point needling, either dry needling or local anaesthetic injection, for persistent active points
Identify and correct perpetuating factors such as poor posture, ergonomic strain, muscle overload and psychological stressors
Use simple analgesia and consider a low-dose tricyclic antidepressant or muscle relaxant for pain and associated sleep disturbance
Screen for and treat contributing conditions including thyroid dysfunction, vitamin deficiency and sleep disturbance
Maintain an active multimodal rehabilitation programme and address central sensitisation in chronic cases
